title: Claiming — Stopping Two Agents Doing One Job

questions.prompt: A worker claims a node like this: `if (task.status === 'ready') { task.status = 'claimed' }`. In a heavy fan-out, two workers still duplicate the work. What is the flaw?
options: The status field is spelled inconsistently
Check and set are two separate steps, so two workers can both read 'ready' before either writes — it needs to be atomic
Workers should re-read the status after writing it
The task needs a longer lease
questions.explanation: Between the read and the write, both workers can observe `ready`, so both proceed; the write is a race, not a lock. Option A is a cosmetic guess. Option C reads the status even later, after the race has happened. Option D helps a *dead* owner, not a simultaneous one, and this bug fires on healthy workers.

questions.prompt: You use exclusive file create for claims, and a worker is killed mid-node. The node never returns to the queue. What is missing?
options: A bigger machine, so workers do not get killed
A lease with an expiry, so a dead owner's claim returns the node to ready
Idempotency, so the node can run twice
A soft edge, so the node does not wait
questions.explanation: A claim record with no expiry is permanent; the lease is what detects a dead owner and frees the node. Option A avoids the symptom, not the mechanism. Option C is necessary for *safe re-run* but does not by itself release the claim. Option D is an edge-classification idea and unrelated to ownership.

questions.prompt: A worker claims a node, edits twelve files, and *then* checks whether it still holds the claim — on discovering it lost the race, it rolls back. Why is this still wrong?
options: Rolling back is impossible, so it should keep the edits
The side effect happened before the claim check, so the rollback itself races with the winner; the check must precede any side effect
It should claim after finishing instead of before
questions.explanation: A claim only protects you if it gates the work; acting first and checking later means two workers can both have edited before either backs out. Option A abandons the guarantee entirely. Option C claims too late to matter. Option D is the tempting equivalence, and it fails precisely because the loser's edits are already on disk.

questions.prompt: A single agent runs a small graph sequentially and someone suggests adding claim files for every node. Overkill, or necessary?
options: Necessary — every graph should use claims
Overkill — with one writer there is no race, so claiming adds state and possible stale leases for nothing
Necessary, because claims also prevent the node running twice
Overkill, but only because single agents cannot revisit nodes
questions.explanation: Claims exist to resolve contention among writers; with one writer there is nothing to contend. Option A is the tempting over-engineering, and stale leases become a new failure mode. Option C is half-right — idempotency helps on resume — but a single sequential run does not resume mid-node, and a claim is not the tool for it. Option D states a false reason.
